caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 140 of 1993
lawyer:
Akhtar Imam with Md. Serajul Haq, Altai Hossain Khan Kazi Md. Shahiqul Hassan and Ranjan Chakravorty, Advocates ----- For the Appellant
Abdur Rab, Advocate ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Bangladesh Telegraph and Telephone Board ----- Appellant
Vs.
Lithi Enterprise Ltd ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Karim, J.: This first miscellaneous appeal at the instance of the defendant is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.1.93 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka, in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 78 of 1990 making the award a Rule of the Court. 

 2. The defendant Bangladesh Telegraph & Telephone Board (hereinafter referred as the BTTB) is the appellant before us and the plaintiff Lithi Enterprise Ltd, a private limited company, is the respondent. BTTB invited a tender for preparation of computerised telephone and telex bills for Dhaka, Chittagong and other areas of the country. The tender of the respondent company being the lowest was accepted by the appellant and accordingly, an agreement was executed between the BTTB and M/s. Lithi Enterprise Ltd on 16.2.88. Clause (1) of the agreement stipulates that on the basis of data to be submitted by BTTB, the respondent company would prepare 2000 telephone and 1000 telex bills on an experimental basis within a period of two months by using the computer of the Atomic Energy Commission and the contract between the parties would come into force for a period of 3 years subject to acceptance of those experimental bills. The respondent company prepared and submitted the experimental bills, but the appellant was not satisfied with the work and refused to accept the same. Ultimately on 12.1.89 BTTB cancelled the agreement. Against the cancellation of the agreement Lithi Enterprise Ltd., the respondent, invoked the arbitration clause of the agreement and asked the BTTB to appoint an Arbitrator for settlement of the dispute, but the BTTB did not comply with this request for arbitration as a result of which the respondent company filed an application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act being Miscellaneous Case No. 78 of 1990 before the learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. BTTB appeared and contested the Miscellaneous Case contending that the case was not maintainable as the respondent company failed to prepare the experimental bills in terms of the agreement within the specified period of 2 months and the bills having not been found acceptable, as per clause (1) of the agreement dated 16.2.88, it stood ineffective and was accordingly cancelled. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing both sides allowed the case and appointed two arbitrators from the lists submitted by both parties for settlement of the dispute and against this decision of the learned Subordinate Judge BTTB filed a revisional application being Civil Revision No. 63 of 1992 and obtained a Rule from a Division Bench of this Court. The Division Bench hearing the Rule came to the conclusion that there existed a dispute between the parties arising out of an agreement containing an arbitration clause and the parties by nominating their arbitrators chose to refer their dispute to arbitration and, as such, the application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act was maintainable. The other point taken by the petitioner in the Civil Revision was that the Division Bench having passed an order on 5.1.92 staying appointment of arbitrators in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 78 of 1990, the filings of the award by the arbitration on 15.1.92 was illegal and without jurisdiction. The Division Bench found that the petitioners did not inform the court below or the arbitrators about the stay or obtained by them on 5.1.92 and accordingly, held that the award filed by the arbitrators was legal and valid in the eye of law. In this view of the matter, the Rule was discharged. Against this order, the BTTB filed civil petition for leave to appeal No. 368 of 1992. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division did not grant leave to appeal leaving these questions for decision by the learned Subordinate Judge. These questions are: first, whether as per clause (1) of the agreement, the provision for arbitration is not applicable because the agreement itself became ineffective; and secondly, whether the two arbitrators appointed by the learned Subordinate Judge, filed the award on 15.1.92 by ignoring the stay order passed on 5.1.92 in Civil Revision No. 63 of 1992. The learned Subordinate Judge did not accept these two points canvassed on behalf of BTTB and found that the award passed by the Arbitrators was valid and in accordance with law and accordingly he made the award Rule of the court. Being aggrieved by this judgment and decree, the defendant has preferred this appeal. 

 7. Mr. Akhtar Imam, learned Advocate for the appellant, submitted that the continuation of the arbitration proceeding and the filing of the award on 15.1.92 after the stay order passed by the Division Bench on 5.1.92 in Civil Revision No. 63 of 1992 has rendered the award invalid and without jurisdiction. In this connection Mr. Imam has referred to the case of Persumai & ors. Vs. Government of Pakistan & ors. reported in PLD 1960 (Karachi) 690 wherein it is held that an order passed by an inferior Court during the subsistence of a stay order made by a superior Court is an absolute nullity. This principle of law is well settled. Mr. Akhtar Imam has next referred to the case of Mst. Umda Begum & another Vs. Saad Saood Jan & others reported in PLD 1962 (Lahore) 306. In that case for failure to pay rent, there was an ejectment proceeding, which was stayed by the appellate authority. It was held by the Division Bench that the ejectment order, while the stay order was in force, is without jurisdiction. There is no dispute about this principle of law. 

 8. Mr. Abdur Rab, learned Advocate for the respondent, has submitted that the stay order obtained in Civil Revision No. 63 of 1992 was not communicated to the learned Subordinate Judge or the two Arbitrators. In his judgment the learned Subordinate Judge has mentioned that no order of stay was communicated to the arbitrators and, in fact, the Arbitrators in their award have mentioned that the only intimation they received from the BTTB was that they would go to the superior Court against the arbitration proceeding without receiving any stay order and, as such, they decided to continue the arbitration proceeding. Ultimately on hearing both sides the Division Bench discharged the Rule in Civil Revision No. 63 of 1992 after being satisfied that the stay order passed by it was not communicated to the court below or the arbitrators and accordingly held that in these circumstances the award filed by the arbitrators was legal and valid in the eye of law. The contention of Mr. Akhtar Imam that the arbitrator filed the award ignoring the stay order passed in Civil Revision No. 63 of 1992 is without any substance. The Arbitrators having been appointed by the learned Subordinate Judge without receipt of any order of stay and similarly the arbitrators having received no such stay order and ultimately the Rule having been discharged by the Division Bench, we find that the facts of the instant case are quite different from those of the two cases referred to by the learned Advocate for the appellant. In this view of the matter, we find that the appointment of the arbitrators and the award submitted by them cannot be considered as invalid. 

 9. Misconduct on the part of the Arbitrators may be a ground for setting aside the award. The judgment passed by the learned Subordinate Judge mentions that no plea of judicial misconduct was made before him and he also did not find any judicial misconduct being committed by the Arbitrators. Mr. Akhtar Imam, learned Advocate for the appellant, has submitted that the agreement dated 16.2.88 is hit by section 21 of the Specific Relief Act and for this he referred to clause (a) and clause (b) of this section. He has argued that a contract for the non- performance of which compensation in money is an adequate relief and further a contract which runs into such minute or numerous details that the Court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms cannot be specifically enforced. In this connection he has referred to the case of Messers MP Ali Mia & Sons Vs. Messers Green and White Ltd. reported in 15 DLR 708 in which it was held by a Division Bench that an award can be set aside on the 'ground of an error of law as being judicial misconduct if the error appears on the face of the award. It is a well settled principle of law and is not disputed by the learned Advocate for the respondent. Mr. Akhtar Imam has further referred to the case of Chhogmal Rawatmal Vs. Sankalchand G. Shah and others reported in 53 CWN 828. In this case a Division Bench held that the arbitrators may be right or they may be wrong but they are entitled to come to a conclusion if there is evidence or if there is material on which they can determine the matter. But in the absence of any evidence or any material or even any allegation to that effect, they are guilty of legal misconduct if they come to any such finding. In this case the arbitrators had before them the agreement dated 16.2.88 and the series of letters sent by the parties, which were considered by them in passing the award. The arbitrators also took into consideration the persistent refusal of BTTB to sit in a joint meeting with the respondent company in order to discuss whether there was really any necessity for preparation of 10,000 telephone and 1000 telex bills for the second time at considerable expense and time. So, it cannot be said that the award of the arbitrators is not based on any material or is bad on that score. 

 10. In this case we may refer to the case of KM Shafi Ltd. Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 1982 BLD 111. In this case decided by a Division Bench of this Court of the two points of dispute referred to the arbitrators, one was whether the costs of materials not consumed and returned by the contractor were deductible under clause 8 of the additional terms and conditions of the contract. The arbitrator took the view that the costs were deductible. The learned Subordinate Judge, who heard the objection against the award, took the view that the arbitrator had construed clause 8 correctly. The Division Bench held that even if the learned Subordinate Judge would have been of a different view he could not have set aside the award on this point on the ground that clause 8 was capable of being interpreted differently and that the arbitrator was the sole judge of construction of the clause. In this connection we may refer to the case of Rising Sun Traders Ltd. Vs. Chittagong Port Authority and another reported in 43 DLR 1, which is a Division Bench decision. Here also the well settled principle of law was reiterated. In proceedings arising out of arbitration, a Court cannot be regarded as a court of appeal from the decision of the arbitrator. It can set aside an award only on the limited ground set forth in section 30 of the Arbitration Act. If an award is otherwise valid a Court cannot interfere with it or review it. In this case we do not find anything to show that the arbitrator has misconducted himself or the proceedings or that the award has been improperly procured or is otherwise invalid. 

 13. It is clear from the facts and circumstances of the case that a dispute between the parties arose out of an agreement dated 16.2.88 and the parties including the appellant chose their arbitrators and submitted to the process of arbitration. In this view of the matter, the contention of Mr. Akhtar Imam that the provision for arbitration as contained in the agreement dated 16.2.88 is not applicable to this case is without any substance. We also find that the arbitrators have not committed misconduct. There is nothing to show that the award is in any way biased or perverse. 

 In the facts and circumstances of the case, we find no substance in this appeal, which should be dismissed. In the result, the appeal is dismissed and the impugned judgment and decree are affirmed.
